name: Carlos Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the injection moulding machines at a plastics plant out past the ring road. We make crates and bottle caps, mostly caps. I start at six, check the hopper's full of pellets, watch the parts drop, pull samples every half hour and measure them with the gauge, and call the setter when something looks off, which is often, because I still can't fix most faults myself. The noise and the heat off the barrels wear you out, but I like the guys on my shift, and I like that at the end of the day there's a pallet you can point at.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you can't fix most faults yourself yet. How long have you been there, and what did you do before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fourteen months. Before that I was eleven years at a furniture warehouse, loading trucks, until they shut it and moved everything to a big automated site three hours away. So I'm forty-three and the new guy, learning from Bogdan, who's sixty-one and can hear a bad mould before he sees it. My partner Ines does home care, our boy Mateo is thirteen and Lucia is nine, and with the mortgage on the 3rd of every month, we've never had more than a few hundred put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, okay. Honestly that sounds like what I already see. They put a robot arm on the boxing station last year and it does the stacking, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, to be honest. In the union group chat everyone's been forwarding these scary videos, and I'd say look, it was a lot of noise and the bosses still need us on the floor. I'd still say we should keep an eye on them, because they'll use any excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if AI is just hype, the robot arms aren't. The boxing station used to be two women, Maria and Fatima, and now it's one arm and a guy who watches three lines. So for me nothing changing still means the slow squeeze I already feel, just no big shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going like now, I suppose. Keep learning the machines from Bogdan so I'm not the first one they let go, keep paying my union dues, keep the overtime when they offer it. There's no money to do anything else anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of relief, but not much. It's like hearing the storm went the other way, but your roof was already leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bosses would use any excuse. Excuse for what, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To hold pay down. Last spring they told us there'd be no raise because of "investment in automation", and that investment was the arm that took Maria's job. So even a boring version of AI becomes a story they tell us at the pay talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to Maria and Fatima?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fatima moved to the night cleaning crew, less money. Maria left, she's doing shifts at the supermarket on the main road now. I see her at the till and she always asks if the arm is still there, like it's a person she doesn't like.

S0.say: AI turned out to be a lot of noise, and the bosses still need us on the floor. But we should keep watching them, because they'll use any story to hold our pay down.
S0.think: Even if AI is hype, the robot arms aren't, and they keep taking jobs one station at a time. For me nothing changing just means the slow squeeze I already feel, without a big shock.
S0.do: Keeps learning the machines from Bogdan so he isn't first out, keeps paying union dues and takes all the overtime offered. Has no spare money to do anything else.
S0.feel: A small relief, but the worry he already carries stays.
S0.quote: It's like hearing the storm went the other way, but your roof was already leaking.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos separates AI from robots very clearly: to him the threat is the arm on the boxing station, not software. Even the calmest scenario reads as a continued squeeze, because he's new, low paid and has almost no savings. Pay talks are where he feels automation most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds more real to me. "Lots of people have to change how they work" is what they always say right before people lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table before any new machine comes in, not after. Online I'd share the stuff about retraining money, because if jobs change then the company and the government should pay for people to learn, not us out of our own pockets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? I'm the guy who'd have to change, and I'm bad at changing. I'm still slow on the touch screen of the new press, I don't use these AI things at all, I don't even like the self-checkout. If they put a screen and a robot on every line, they keep the young ones who swipe fast and the old ones who know everything, and I'm in the middle with neither.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to Kemal, our shop steward, and push for a written deal that nobody gets let go without training first. At home we'd cut the extras: the football club fees for Mateo hurt to think about, but the streaming and the takeaway on Fridays go first. I wouldn't sign up for some course on my own, I don't trust them, and I can't pay for one anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like I'm back at the warehouse in the last months, when everyone knew and nobody said it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't sign up for a course on your own. If the company paid and gave you the hours, would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's paid and in work time, yes, I'd go. I wouldn't like it, I'd sit at the back, but I'd go. What I won't do is give up Saturdays and pay some online thing that promises the moon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ines that evening, if the company announced it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight, she always knows anyway. She'd say "again?" and then we'd sit at the kitchen table with the bank statements, like we did when the warehouse closed. I'd tell her the union is on it, and she'd tell me the union didn't save the warehouse.

S1.say: The union has to be at the table before any new machine comes in, not after. If jobs change, the company and the government should pay for people to learn.
S1.think: I'm the guy who'd have to change, and I'm bad at changing. They'd keep the young ones who swipe fast and the old ones who know everything, and I'm stuck in the middle without either.
S1.do: Goes to the shop steward to push for a written no-layoffs-without-training deal. Cuts streaming and Friday takeaways at home, and would only take a course if the company pays and it's in work time.
S1.feel: Tight-chested and familiar dread, the same as the last months at the warehouse.
S1.quote: They keep the young ones who swipe fast and the old ones who know everything, and I'm in the middle with neither.
S1.fieldNote: This is where his resistance to new tech and his politics meet. He wants change to be negotiated collectively and paid for by others, partly from principle and partly because he can't afford anything himself. Ines's line about the union not saving the warehouse shows his faith in collective action is real but bruised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Mateo would be fifteen. That's… okay. Give me a second, that one's a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let a handful of tech billionaires decide everything, and that every government that let it happen should be ashamed. I'd be at the protests, I'd be sharing everything. I'd say they need to tax the robots and pay people, because what else is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished. I'm the newest guy on a line that a robot can already half run. If it can do anything a person does and it's cheaper, there's no warehouse three hours away to move to this time, because there's nothing left anywhere. With what we have saved, we miss one mortgage payment and the letters start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and every march, that's the one thing I know how to do. I'd call the bank the first month to ask about pausing the mortgage, before we're behind, not after. Ines's job in home care might last a bit longer, so we'd lean on that, and on her sister, who has a spare room. We'd stop everything that isn't food, the house and the kids' school things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor drops out. I don't think I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Ines's sister's spare room. Are you saying you'd think about moving in there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to it. Four of us in one room in her flat on the other side of town, the kids changing schools. I'd hate it, I'd feel like a failure in front of my own kids. But better than the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bogdan, strangely. Everyone thinks he's safe because he's the best, but sixty-one and the best at something a robot does better is still nothing. He told me once he's got nothing outside that place, his wife passed. I'd worry what he'd do with his days.

S2.say: This is what happens when a few tech billionaires decide everything and governments let them. Tax the robots and pay people, because there's nothing else left.
S2.think: Honestly, I think I'm finished: I'm the newest guy on a line a robot already half runs, and there's nowhere left to move to. With what we've saved, one missed mortgage payment and the letters start.
S2.do: Goes to every union meeting and march, and calls the bank in the first month to ask about pausing the mortgage. Leans on Ines's income and her sister's spare room, and stops all spending beyond food, the house and school things.
S2.feel: Like the floor drops out, with no sleep and a deep fear of failing his kids.
S2.quote: Sixty-one and the best at something a robot does better is still nothing.
S2.fieldNote: With two years' warning Carlos sees no personal way out, only collective protest and family. He moved fast to practical damage control, calling the bank before falling behind, which suggests he learned from the warehouse closure. His worry for Bogdan says a lot about how he sees skill: it doesn't protect you if the machine is better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's still fast, but it's not tomorrow. Lucia would be fourteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: tax it, share it, and give unions a say in how it's brought in. But with five years I'd be pushing harder for things to get written into law before it lands, like a guaranteed income or a long notice period. I'd tell people to vote on it, not just complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, five years mostly means five years of watching it come. I don't think I'd become a different person in that time. I'm not going to turn into a programmer. But maybe there's time to pay a bit off the house, and time for the politicians to do something, if enough of us shout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put something aside every month, even fifty, which sounds like nothing but we've never had a habit of it. I'd do more union work, maybe stand as a rep if Kemal asked. I'd go and vote and drag my brother along. I'd still not chase every course they advertise, but if the union got one paid, I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but I can breathe. It's dread, but it's dread with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years is mostly watching it come. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every time a new machine comes in the gate, you wonder. Every time management walks the floor with people in clean jackets, you wonder. I'd be looking at the robot arm every morning thinking, which one of us are you this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save fifty a month. Where would that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, from me smoking less, and from Ines and me not doing the cinema. The kids' stuff I'd try to keep. That's the deal I made with myself after the warehouse: the kids don't pay for it if I can help it.

S3.say: Tax it, share it, and give unions a say in how it comes in. With five years, we should get a guaranteed income and long notice periods written into law before it lands.
S3.think: Five years mostly means five years of watching it come, and I won't turn into a different person. But maybe there's time to pay a bit off the house, and for politicians to act if enough of us shout.
S3.do: Saves even fifty a month by smoking less and dropping the cinema, and does more union work, maybe standing as a rep. Votes and gets his brother to vote; takes a course only if the union gets it paid.
S3.feel: Heavy dread, but with room to breathe and a sense of having a plan.
S3.quote: I'd be looking at the robot arm every morning thinking, which one of us are you this year.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time doesn't change who Carlos is; it changes where he puts his energy, from protest to law and voting. He still won't retrain on his own. The small deal he made with himself, that the kids don't pay for it, is the most personal thing he said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be fifty-three. Mateo would be grown, Lucia almost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for the government to get ready, so no excuses this time. People like me need a plan made for us, not a leaflet telling us to "reskill". I'd keep saying that at union meetings and anywhere anyone listens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is better for me, I'll admit it. The kids would be mostly through school, maybe we'd have the worst of the mortgage behind us. But at fifty-three, who hires a man who never learned the screens? It just moves my bad day further down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down at work and get properly good at the presses, because the good ones go last. Keep at the union and keep voting for whoever promises a real safety net. Put a bit away when there's overtime. Mostly, honestly, I'd wait and see what the government actually does, because there's no point me guessing alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, still. But it's the worry you live with, not the one that wakes you at three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get properly good at the presses. Isn't that a strange thing to invest in, if robots take over in the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But it's what I've got. If I'm the best on the line in year eight, I'm still there in year nine. That's one more year of the mortgage paid, one more year of Lucia's school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about choosing work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mateo don't do what I did, don't pick a job because it's there. Do something with people, like your mum, or something where you fix the machines, not feed them. And join a union, wherever you go.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for the government to get ready, so no excuses this time. People like me need a real plan made for us, not a leaflet telling us to reskill.
S4.think: Ten years is easier for me: the kids would be mostly through school and the mortgage lighter. But at fifty-three, who hires a man who never learned the screens? It just moves my bad day down the road.
S4.do: Gets properly good at the presses so he's among the last to go, and keeps up union work and voting for a real safety net. Saves overtime money and mostly waits to see what the government does.
S4.feel: A background worry he can live with, not one that wakes him at night.
S4.quote: Do something with people, like your mum, or something where you fix the machines, not feed them.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years helps Carlos mainly because of his kids' ages, not because he'd use it to change. He makes a reasoned case for getting better at a job that may vanish: each extra year is a year of the mortgage. His advice to Mateo shows he knows the difference between fixing machines and feeding them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is time and money, really: a guarantee that if they take the job, the mortgage gets paused and there's an income while things settle. And unions having a say in how fast it comes in, so it isn't just the owners deciding on a Tuesday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids much, not how they feel. Mateo asked me last week if robots will take my job, because he saw a video. I said no. I don't know if that was a lie.

headlineQuote: Mateo asked me last week if robots will take my job, because he saw a video. I said no. I don't know if that was a lie.
portrait: Carlos is forty-three, fourteen months into running injection moulding machines at a plastics plant after his warehouse job was automated away. He's a union man who distrusts bosses and tech billionaires, slow with screens, and won't use AI tools or pay for courses himself. Across the scenarios his answer is always collective: the union, the vote, tax the robots. The fast AGI picture leaves him panicked and thinking about moving his family into his sister-in-law's spare room, while ten years helps mainly because his kids would be grown.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be the newest worker on a line a robot already half runs, with no savings and nowhere left to go.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee that the mortgage is paused and an income paid if the job goes, and unions having a say in how fast automation comes in.
